entries.title: Korean at a glance
body: Korean puts the verb last (subject, object, verb) and marks each noun's role with a particle after it, much like Japanese. Endings stack onto verbs to show tense, politeness and mood.
Hangul was created under King Sejong and published in 1446 so that ordinary people could read and write. It is an alphabet whose letters are grouped into one block per syllable.

entries.title: Syllable blocks
body: Every block starts with a consonant; ㅇ is silent at the start of a block so that a syllable can begin with a vowel. Tall vowels (ㅏ ㅓ ㅣ) go to the right of the first consonant, flat ones (ㅗ ㅜ ㅡ) go below. A final consonant (batchim) sits at the bottom.
There are 14 basic consonants and 10 basic vowels, plus doubled consonants and combined vowels.

examples.e: consonant, tall vowel to the right, final at the bottom
consonant, flat vowel below, final at the bottom
silent ㅇ in front of a vowel

entries.title: Why the letters look the way they do
body: The basic consonants are drawn after the speech organs that make them, and extra strokes add aspiration: ㄱ → ㅋ, ㄷ → ㅌ, ㅈ → ㅊ.
The vowels are built from three symbols: a dot for heaven, a flat line (ㅡ) for earth and an upright line (ㅣ) for people. The dot has become a short stroke: ㅏ ㅓ ㅗ ㅜ.

head: Letter
Shape shows
rows: the back of the tongue touching the soft palate
the tongue tip touching the ridge behind the teeth

entries.title: Plain, aspirated and tense consonants
entries.body: Korean splits stops into three: plain (lightly breathy), aspirated (a strong puff of air) and tense (tight throat, no puff). English speakers need to practise hearing the difference.

entries.title: Final consonants and linking
body: At the end of a syllable, consonants are not released and collapse to seven sounds: k, n, t, l, m, p, ng. So 옷, 옫 and 옺 all sound like ot.
When the next syllable starts with silent ㅇ, the final consonant slides over and is said in full.

examples.e: clothes (+ subject particle): ㅅ moves over

entries.title: 은/는 and 이/가
body: Particles have one form after a consonant and another after a vowel. {은/는} marks the topic, often for contrast or known information. {이/가} marks the subject, especially new information or the answer to who or what.
Use the first form after a final consonant (책은, 책이) and the second after a vowel (저는, 친구가).

examples.e: I am a student. (as for me…)

head: Particle
Marks
Example
rows: 밥을 먹어요 · eat a meal; 커피를 마셔요 · drink coffee
학교에 가요 · go to school; 세 시에 · at three
도서관에서 공부해요 · study at the library
제 친구의 집 · my friend's house

entries.title: Speech levels
entries.body: Korean verbs end differently depending on who you're talking to. The polite -요 style is the safe default with adults you don't know well. The formal -ㅂ니다 style is for news, announcements, presentations and the army. Casual speech (drop -요) is for close friends, younger people and family.

entries.title: The polite present: -아요 / -어요
entries.body: Take the dictionary form, drop -다, and add -아요 if the last vowel of the stem is ㅏ or ㅗ, or -어요 otherwise. Vowels merge where they meet, and every 하다 verb becomes 해요.

entries.title: Past tense and negatives
body: Past: replace -아요 / -어요 with -았어요 / -었어요; 해요 becomes 했어요.
Not: put {안} before the verb, or add {-지 않아요} to the stem. Can't: put {못} before the verb, or add -지 못해요. With 하다 verbs, 안 and 못 go before 하다: 공부 안 해요.

entries.title: To be: 이에요 / 예요 and 아니에요
entries.body: Attach 이에요 to a noun ending in a consonant and 예요 to a noun ending in a vowel. The negative is 아니에요, with 이/가 on the noun.

entries.title: Two number systems
body: {Sino-Korean} numbers (from Chinese) are used for dates, money, minutes, phone numbers and floors. {Native Korean} numbers are used for counting things and people, age and hours, up to 99.
Before a counter, 하나, 둘, 셋, 넷 and 스물 shorten to 한, 두, 세, 네 and 스무.

entries.title: Honorifics
body: Korean shows respect to the person you talk about as well as to the listener. Add {-시-} to a verb when its subject deserves respect, and use 씨 or 님 after names and titles rather than the bare name.
Some words have their own honorific forms: 드시다 (eat), 주무시다 (sleep), 계시다 (be, stay), 연세 (age), 성함 (name).

examples.e: Goodbye (to someone staying, when you leave).

entries.title: Want to: -고 싶어요
entries.body: Add -고 싶어요 to a verb stem to say what you want to do. For other people, use -고 싶어해요.

examples.e: I want to go to Korea.

entries.title: Future: -(으)ㄹ 거예요
entries.body: Add -ㄹ 거예요 to a stem ending in a vowel and -을 거예요 to one ending in a consonant. It means will or am going to.

examples.e: I'm going to eat gimbap for lunch.

entries.title: Joining clauses: -고, -지만, -아서/어서
entries.body: Korean links clauses with endings on the first verb, not separate words. The tense usually goes only on the last verb.

head: Ending
Meaning
Example
rows: 밥을 먹고 공부했어요 · I ate and studied
비싸지만 좋아요 · it's expensive but good
배가 고파서 먹었어요 · I was hungry, so I ate
